body.text: The end of the Cold War, followed by the the dissolution of the Soviet Union, marked a turning point for Türkiye in redefining and developing its relations with the Turkic republics of Central Asia and the Caucasus.

Türkiye was the first country to recognize the independence of the Turkic republics of Central Asia. While Ankara’s policies toward the region took shape amid the uncertainties that emerged following the end of the bipolar order, the Central Asian countries, for their part, prioritized areas such as nation-building, the transition to a market economy, and economic reforms during this process.

Relations among the countries in the region had not yet fully taken shape during that initial post-independence period. Thirty-five years after the Central Asian republics gained independence, both the international system and Türkiye’s foreign policy have changed significantly.

As the post-Cold War order has given way to multipolar competition and greater regional initiatives, Ankara has adopted a foreign policy that places increasing emphasis on regional cooperation, economic interconnectivity, and soft power strategies – a policy that, within this framework, is multidimensional, proactive, and seeks autonomy. This change has coincided with the deepening of cooperation among the Central Asian states. For example, some Central Asian republics – such as Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan – can now travel to each other’s countries using only their national ID cards. Furthermore, by taking constructive steps to resolve certain water and border disputes, they have come to recognize the importance of regional cooperation.
The Organization of Turkic States (OTS) has thus regained strategic importance and momentum amid this broad and comprehensive process of transformation.

In this context, the 13th Summit of the Organization of Turkic States, held in Ankara on October 29-30, 2026, under the theme “The Turkic Century: Unity in Language, Thought, and Deed,” marked a turning point in the organization’s institutionalization.

The Summit process of the Leaders of Turkic-Speaking States, which began in Ankara in late October 1992, laid the foundations for regular political dialogue and mutual trust among the countries. Subsequently, the Nakhchivan Agreement, signed in 2009, transformed this political will into a permanent institutional structure. Finally, at the 2021 Istanbul Summit, the name of the Turkic Council was changed to the Organization of Turkic States, and the “Turkic World 2040 Vision” was adopted; this was a concrete indication that the organization had become much more than a symbolic entity.

The timing of the Ankara Summit – October 29-30 – also held its own significance as the opening day coincided with Türkiye’s Republic Day, bringing to mind the phrase “respect for the past, a legacy for the future.”
So, why is the Ankara Summit important, and what contribution has it made to this process?

The 163-article Ankara Declaration, the 2026 summit’s main outcome, outlined as a priority cooperation in the areas of defense, cybersecurity, trade, energy, education, and transportation. With this summit, Türkiye assumed the rotating chairmanship from Azerbaijan. In assuming the rotating presidency, Türkiye’s primary task is to translate the political will expressed at the summit into action-oriented programs and measurable results over the next year.

One of the most notable proposals in the declaration is the establishment of an OTS Defense Industry College, to be hosted by Türkiye in accordance with the defense industry roadmap agreed upon in Baku on October 1. This project demonstrates that the organization seeks to forge ties not only through cultural affinity but also in the areas of joint production and defense. Regarding cybersecurity, they called for accelerating consultations on the Cybersecurity Council and a memorandum of understanding.

Transportation was another key topic at the summit. The communiqué addressed the Middle Corridor connecting Central Asia and Europe, the more efficient use of the Baku-Tbilisi-Kars railway, the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway currently under construction, and the Zangezur Corridor. Kazakh President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev announced the launch of the Trans-Caspian fiber-optic cable between Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan, which is also open to other Turkic states; this serves as an example of how the agenda in question can be realized on the ground. Meanwhile, Uzbekistan’s “Turkic World-100” program-comprising 100 joint investment and industrial projects covering critical minerals and green technology – also reflects a similar level of seriousness. The call to complete the production phase and accelerate the launch of the jointly developed 12U OTS-SAT CubeSat satellite stands among the organization’s first concrete steps in the space sector.

The issue of regional travel was the agenda item of greatest interest to citizens of the OTS member states at the summit. Uzbekistan’s President Shavkat Mirziyoyev called for the conclusion of a multilateral agreement on mutual travel among OTS member states, the wider use of ID cards at border crossings, and the simplification of border procedures and length of stay in host countries. Furthermore, Mirziyoyev proposed the establishment of a “Tourism Alliance of Turkic-Speaking Countries.” This idea is not new: at an informal summit held in Turkistan in May, the OTS announced that it was working on a “Turkic ID Card” project, with the support of Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan. In other words, the call for concrete steps toward the creation of a “Turkic Schengen” has been reiterated.

In the realm of “linguistic unity,” Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan proposed the development of a joint digital trade platform and large language model for Turkic languages. Additionally, Mirziyoyev proposed the creation of a joint dictionary of Turkic languages.

The summit’s institutional outcomes are also quite significant. Uzbekistan’s Deputy Foreign Minister Mirvokhid Azimov was appointed as the new secretary-general of the OTS, replacing Kubanychbek Omuraliev; Uzbekistan will host the next summit in 2027, while Kyrgyzstan has requested to organize an informal summit that same year. Regarding expansion, Mirziyoyev’s call for an “OTS Plus” format and Tokayev’s proposal to invite Russia to participate in this format or as an observer drew attention, though no decision has been announced.

The Ankara summit showcases an organization that has found its stride. In a single meeting, the OTS addressed issues ranging from defense and space to trade, energy, and even citizens’ freedom of travel.

It would have been difficult for the leaders who first gathered in Ankara in 1992 to even imagine such a broad range of topics. The foundations are already visible: a joint defense industry roadmap, a CubeSat satellite ready for launch, a fiber-optic line connecting Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan, and a proposed travel agreement based on a model already in operation between Uzbekistan and Kyrgyzstan. The Turkish Investment Fund and the Middle Corridor – for which Uzbekistan has proposed channeling its resources into the “Turkic World-100” program – offer practical avenues for the growth of these goals.

The political environment is equally important: a regular summit schedule that continues to bring member states to the table, a new secretary-general from Uzbekistan, and the rotating presidency, which has now passed to Türkiye and is returning with renewed momentum.

Another source of optimism lies in their historical origins. Unlike European states that began the process of integration after centuries of interstate rivalry and destructive wars, the member states of the OTS do not carry a legacy of deep hostility at the state level. They share a long common heritage, close linguistic and cultural affinities, and overlapping historical memories – a foundation that European integration has built at great cost. Although the OTS is a much younger organization than the European Union, this starting point suggests that as its institutions mature, it will be able to move smoothly toward deeper integration.
